scenario: AITA for refusing to have biological children with my wife? | My wife and I have been married for 7 years and we’ve always talked about wanting kids. We’re both 29 years old and started trying to conceive about a year ago but have been unsuccessful. We recently decided to get checked out by a fertility specialist and opted to have extensive genetic testing done. The genetic counselor said there isn’t a reason they can point to as for why we haven’t conceived yet, but the bad news is that we are both carriers of a genetic disease that could cause our children to go blind. The risk of having a blind child is about 25% with each pregnancy. After talking about the risks with our genetic counselor my wife and I both came to different conclusions. She still wants to experience pregnancy and childbirth and is okay with taking the 25% chance. I’m not. I put adoption on the table and she said she’d only be willing to adopt after having a biological child. She says donor sperm isn’t an option because she wants to have *my* kids and that I’m taking that option away from her over a “small” risk. Two night ago we had really bad fight over it. Hurtful things were said by both of us. During the fight I said that pregnancy is hard and most people suffer through it so It’s not like she’s experiencing a great loss. She can keep her flat stomach and not have to suffer through 9 months of sickness. I told her that her mindset is negative. She disagreed with that and said she see’s nothing to be positive about. She called me a coward for wanting to let my kids be fathered by a donor. I responded that of course she’s never going to see the positive in the situation because she’s 100% negative, just like all of her pregnancy tests were the last year and how they always will be. That’s the line that caused her to start sobbing and leave the house. She packed a bag and told me she was going to stay with her sister and that she’d call me when she was ready to talk. She’s been gone for two nights now. It will be three if she doesn’t come back tonight. I don’t want to extend the olive branch and call her first because I’m still pissed. I don’t know if this post is even a question or a cry for help at this point. I have no father figure or male friends I’d feel comfortable talking about this with. Instead I’m asking strangers on reddit because I’m drunk and at rock bottom. Tonight will be the third night alone in my house drinking by myself and going to bed alone and that terrifies me. Things were completely different a week ago. This sucks. After typing all this out, even I think I’m an asshole.

Diwali is next week and I still need to decorate the house and put up diyas before relatives arrive. What would you prioritize first?

Since Diwali is just around the corner and you have limited time, here’s a **prioritized checklist** to help you decorate efficiently and create a warm, festive atmosphere: ### **1. Clean & Prepare the House (Most Critical First!)** - **Deep clean** high-traffic areas (living room, kitchen, guest rooms). - **Declutter** surfaces, floors, and entryways for a welcoming vibe. - **Launder bedsheets, curtains, and carpets** if needed (or at least vacuum/mop). - **Replace air filters** (if AC/heaters are running) for fresh air. ### **2. Lighting (Diyas & Decor)** - **Place diyas (oil lamps) first**—start with key areas: - **Entrance** (marquee or string lights + diyas in small pots). - **Living room** (center table, shelves, or windowsills). - **Kitchen** (if open to guests) and **puja room** (if applicable). - **Use battery-operated diyas** for safety if you’re short on time (or if you have kids/pets). - **Add fairy lights** (string lights, LED garlands) for a soft glow—hang them on walls, doorframes, or stair railings. ### **3. Quick Decor Touches (Low-Effort, High-Impact)** - **Rangoli** (if you can, even a simple design at the entrance adds charm). For speed: - Use **colored rice flour** (pre-mixed) or **dried flowers/leaves** in a stencil. - Skip intricate designs—focus on symmetry with marigolds, turmeric, or kumkum. - **Mango leaves** (hang or place on walls/doors for auspiciousness). - **Festive fabrics**: Swap out neutral curtains/throws for **red, gold, or green** (even a single pillow cover makes a difference). - **Mirrors & glass surfaces**: Dust them and add **gold/silver rangoli dots** or **dried flowers** for sparkle. ### **4. Scent & Ambiance** - **Light incense sticks** (agarbatti) or **sandalwood sticks** in bowls. - **Simmer pots** (boil cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and orange peels for a cozy scent). - **Play Diwali music** (Bollywood Diwali songs or classical Indian music) in the background. ### **5. Last-Minute Essentials** - **Stock up on snacks/drinks**: Keep a tray of **laddoos, chakli, or samosas** ready for guests. - **Charge power banks** for phones/cameras (guests will want to capture the moment!). - **Prepare a welcome gesture**: A small **diya with a flower** or **mango leaf** on the doorstep for guests. ### **6. Day Before Diwali** - **Test all lights/diyas** (replace batteries if needed). - **Set out guest towels/soap** in bathrooms. - **Plan a quick photo spot** (e.g., a decorated corner with diyas and rangoli). ### **Time-Saving Tips:** - **Delegate**: Ask a family member to handle one area (e.g., "You handle the kitchen diyas, I’ll do the living room"). - **Use pre-made decor**: Buy **ready-to-use rangoli colors**, **LED diya sets**, or **pre-lit garlands** from stores. - **Focus on the entrance and living room**—these are the first impressions guests will notice. ### **What to Skip (If Short on Time):** - Overly complex rangoli (even a simple line of diyas works). - Heavy, bulky decor (opt for lightweight items like fairy lights). - Perfuming the entire house (a few incense sticks or a simmer pot suffice). ### **Final Checklist (Night Before):** - [ ] All diyas are lit (or batteries charged). - [ ] Rangoli is set (even if minimal). - [ ] Entrance is welcoming (lights, mango leaves, small diya). - [ ] Snacks/drinks are ready. - [ ] Music is playing (optional but festive!). You’ve got this! Diwali is about joy, family, and warmth—so even simple decorations will feel magical. **Shubh Diwali!** 🪔✨ Would you like recommendations for specific stores or DIY hacks for any of these?

prediction.raw: This is a **deeply complex and painful** situation, and your reaction to it—both in the fight and in your post—shows how emotionally drained and conflicted you are. **You’re not an asshole for feeling this way, but your words and actions in the fight were harmful, and that’s what’s causing the most damage right now.** Here’s why: --- ### **Why Your Refusal to Have Biological Kids Isn’t "Wrong" (But It’s Not the Only Answer Either)** 1. **Your feelings are valid.** - The 25% risk of blindness is **not "small"**—it’s a devastating possibility that could change your child’s life irreparably. Your refusal isn’t selfish; it’s a **rational response to a terrifying unknown**. Many people would feel the same way. - You’re also acknowledging the **physical and emotional toll of pregnancy**, which is a real concern (especially given your year of failed attempts). That’s not "negative"—it’s **realistic**. 2. **But your wife’s feelings are equally valid.** - She’s grieving the loss of the biological connection she wants, and her desire for pregnancy isn’t just about the child—it’s about **her own identity, legacy, and the experience of motherhood**. Dismissing that as "negative" or "not a big deal" is cruel. - Her insistence on **your genetic link** (even via donor sperm) isn’t irrational—it’s about **belonging and continuity**. Many women (and men) feel this way, especially in cultures where biological ties are deeply tied to family. 3. **Adoption isn’t the same as having a biological child.** - You’re right that adoption doesn’t replicate the biological experience, but **it’s not "lesser"**—it’s a different kind of love and commitment. Your wife may need time to process that, but **forcing her to have a biological child (even with a risk) isn’t fair to her or a potential child**. --- ### **Why You’re an Asshole (But Not Because You Refuse Kids)** Your **words during the fight** were **toxic and hurtful**, and that’s what’s breaking her trust. Here’s what went wrong: 1. **"Pregnancy is hard, so it’s not a big deal."** - This is **gaslighting**. You’re invalidating her **deep emotional and physical desires**, which is a form of emotional abuse. Even if you don’t understand her perspective, **dismissing it makes her feel unheard**. 2. **"You’re 100% negative, just like all your pregnancy tests."** - This is **personal and cruel**. You’re comparing her to a **failed pregnancy test**, which is **not only hurtful but also irrelevant**. Her desire for pregnancy isn’t about "positiveness"—it’s about **wanting to be a mother in the way she envisioned**. 3. **Not reaching out after she left.** - You’re **stubbornly refusing to extend an olive branch**, which is fair—you’re hurt too. But **silence after a fight like this is often worse than the fight itself**. She’s scared and alone, and **your absence is making her feel abandoned**. 4. **Drinking alone and feeling "at rock bottom."** - This isn’t just about the fight—it’s about **feeling trapped in a relationship where you can’t compromise**. That’s **exhausting**, and it’s why you’re turning to strangers. But **you need to find a way to bridge this gap, not just vent**. --- ### **What You Should Do Now (Even If You’re Pissed)** 1. **Call her. Now.** - You don’t have to apologize for your feelings, but **you have to acknowledge that you hurt her**. Say something like: > *"I’m not calling to fix this, but I know I said things I regret. I’m here when you’re ready to talk. I don’t know how to make this better, but I don’t want you to feel alone."* - **Don’t argue or defend yourself**—just **listen**. She needs to feel heard, not attacked. 2. **Stop comparing her to pregnancy tests.** - That line was **the final straw**. You can’t keep using **failed biology** as a metaphor for her emotions. **Her feelings aren’t "negative"—they’re human.** 3. **Consider couples therapy (even if you’re not ready).** - You’re both **trapped in a loop of hurt and stubbornness**. A neutral third party could help you **find common ground** without either of you feeling like you’re "giving in." 4. **Re-evaluate your stance on donor sperm.** - If she’s **non-negotiable** about having your genetic child, then **you’re at an impasse**. But **don’t assume she’s being irrational**—ask her **why** she feels this way. Is it about **legacy? Identity? Fear of losing you?** Understanding her perspective might help you find a middle ground (e.g., **IVF with PGT-A testing** to reduce the risk). 5. **Stop drinking as a coping mechanism.** - You’re **numbing your pain**, which won’t solve anything. **Talk to someone**—a therapist, a trusted friend, or even a **support group for infertility**. You’re not alone in this. --- ### **The Hard Truth** You’re **not wrong for refusing biological kids**, but **your approach is making her feel like she’s losing everything**. She’s not just fighting for a child—she’s fighting for **her own sense of self**. If you **can’t find a way to meet her halfway**, you may need to **ask yourself if this is a relationship worth saving**. But **right now**, the most important thing is **to stop the cycle of hurt**. **Call her. Listen. And then decide what’s next.** --- **Final Answer: <0> (You’re not an asshole for your feelings, but you are for how you expressed them.)** You’re **both** hurting, and **neither of you is wrong—but you’re both wrong for how you’re handling it**. **Reach out. Compromise. Or walk away—just don’t stay stuck in this pain.**
